hypothesis: N-Acetyl-D-quinovosamine (QuiNAc; KEGG C15481) is increased or characteristic in 12-month-old infants receiving meat-based complementary protein relative to dairy-based complementary protein.
rationale: Extensive searching located no study - human, animal, or in vitro - that reports N-acetyl-D-quinovosamine (or its nucleotide-activated form UDP-QuiNAc) as a measured metabolite differing between meat- and dairy-based complementary feeding, nor any report of this compound in infant fecal or serum metabolomes at all. What the literature does establish is only compound-level/pathway-level background: QuiNAc (2-acetamido-2,6-dideoxy-D-glucose) is a rare bacterial amino sugar that occurs almost exclusively in cell-envelope glycans (O-antigen/LPS, lipooligosaccharide, wall glycopolymers) of Gram-negative and some Gram-positive bacteria (Rhizobium etli, Campylobacter jejuni, Pseudomonas, Bacillus cereus), and is derived from UDP-GlcNAc by 4,6-dehydration/4-reduction. Separately, the meat- vs. dairy-based complementary feeding RCT paradigm in 5-12-month-old U.S. formula-fed infants is well documented (Tang/Krebs trial, with 16S, metagenomic, fecal-metabolomic and blood-metabolomic outputs), and one analysis of that trial reports the meat group being enriched for microbial genes in amino-acid/amino-sugar-related metabolic categories - but no publication I could retrieve names quinovosamine or any specific bacterial deoxy-amino-sugar as a meat-associated metabolite. The only conceivable supporting chain is indirect and speculative (meat-associated diets/taxa such as Acinetobacter and other Gram-negatives could raise LPS-type sugar pools; Campylobacter, a poultry/meat-associated organism, synthesizes Qui3N-containing lipooligosaccharide), which is theoretical reasoning rather than evidence for this feature+group combination. Under the rubric this is weak (1), not 0 (relevant background literature was found) and not -1 (nothing reports the opposite direction for this feature and group either).

evidence.title: In vitro biosynthesis and chemical identification of UDP-N-acetyl-d-quinovosamine (UDP-d-QuiNAc)
evidence.study_population: In vitro bacterial enzymology (no human or animal subjects)
evidence.relevance: Establishes the compound's identity and origin: QuiNAc occurs in polysaccharide structures of many Gram-negative bacteria and is made from UDP-GlcNAc, supporting a bacterial-glycan (not dietary/host) source for this feature - but says nothing about infant diet groups.

evidence.title: The Biosynthesis of UDP-d-QuiNAc in Bacillus cereus ATCC 14579
evidence.relevance: Describes QuiNAc as a relatively rare amino sugar residue found in glycans of a limited set of (mainly pathogenic) bacteria, indicating that its abundance in a gut sample would track specific bacterial taxa rather than protein source per se; no diet or infant data.

evidence.title: Synthesis of N-acetyl-d-quinovosamine in Rhizobium etli CE3 is completed after its 4-keto-precursor is linked to a carrier lipid
evidence.study_population: Bacterial genetics/biochemistry (Rhizobium etli), no human subjects
evidence.relevance: Confirms QuiNAc as the initiating O-antigen sugar of an LPS model system, reinforcing that the metabolite is a microbial cell-envelope building block; provides only pathway-level, non-dietary context.

evidence.title: Characterization of the dTDP-Fuc3N and dTDP-Qui3N biosynthetic pathways in Campylobacter jejuni 81116
evidence.relevance: Links quinovosamine-type sugars to lipooligosaccharide of a meat/poultry-associated enteric organism - the closest, but still highly indirect and speculative, mechanistic bridge to a meat-based diet; not a metabolomic or infant study.

evidence.title: Different gut microbiota in U.S. formula-fed infants consuming a meat vs. dairy-based complementary foods: A randomized controlled trial
evidence.study_population: Full-term, formula-fed U.S. infants randomized to meat- vs. dairy-based complementary diet, 5-12 months (stool at 5, 10, 12 months)
evidence.relevance: Directly matches the study group/exposure (12-month meat vs. dairy complementary protein) and reports microbiota and SCFA outcomes, but does not report N-acetyl-D-quinovosamine or related bacterial amino sugars, so it neither supports nor contradicts the hypothesis.

evidence.title: Different Blood Metabolomics Profiles in Infants Consuming a Meat- or Dairy-Based Complementary Diet
evidence.study_population: Infants in a controlled feeding trial, meat- vs. dairy-based complementary diet 5-12 months, follow-up at 24 months (serum metabolomics)
evidence.relevance: The most directly relevant metabolomic comparison of meat vs. dairy complementary feeding; discriminating metabolites reported are amino acids (e.g., isoleucine, valine, phenylalanine, threonine), with no mention of quinovosamine or bacterial deoxy-amino sugars.

evidence.title: Network-based representation learning reveals the impact of age and diet on the gut microbial and metabolomic environment of U.S. infants in a randomized controlled feeding trial
evidence.study_population: U.S. formula-fed infants, 5-12 months, randomized meat vs. dairy complementary feeding; fecal metagenomics + metabolomics
evidence.relevance: Reports diet- and age-associated enrichment of microbial functions including amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism (the pathway that generates UDP-GlcNAc-derived sugars such as QuiNAc), giving only pathway-level, non-compound-specific plausibility for the hypothesis.

caveats: No literature exists on this specific metabolite in an infant diet or fecal-metabolome context, so the score reflects absence of feature-specific evidence rather than a refutation. Two practical concerns: (1) annotation reliability - QuiNAc is an isomer of N-acetylglucosamine/N-acetylgalactosamine-family and other C8H15NO5 hexosamine derivatives (e.g., N-acetylfucosamine, N-acetyl-deoxyhexosamines), and untargeted LC-MS annotation at this mass without an authentic standard or MS/MS match is easily confounded; the 'metabolite_lipid'/lipid-platform annotation type for a polar amino sugar further raises the chance of misannotation. (2) Even if correctly annotated, QuiNAc is a bacterial cell-envelope sugar, so any diet difference would most plausibly be a downstream marker of taxa composition (e.g., Gram-negative/Proteobacterial load) rather than of meat protein itself, and direction could reverse with cohort or sequencing/metabolomics platform. A search-tool usage limit was reached, so a small number of additional planned queries (e.g., targeted full-text search of the meat/dairy trial's fecal metabolomics supplementary tables) could not be completed; these could in principle surface the compound in a supplementary feature list.evidence found either way at this time.
